HOME AND DAILY LIFE LESSON · HOME AND DAILY LIFE · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Sounds Around Home — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the house&rsquo;s self-made soundtrack: the sounds nobody switches on, from footsteps to creaks to drips — and the news each one carries.

What is this?

The sounds around home: footsteps tip-tapping, the door&rsquo;s creak, the clock&rsquo;s tick, the tap&rsquo;s running (the faucet, across the ocean), the phone&rsquo;s ring.

What does it mean?

Sound-reading is a safety skill wearing a game&rsquo;s clothes: footsteps say who is coming, a running tap says somebody left it on, a creak says which door. Ears that read the house are useful ears.

What does the child need to know?

You need the card and the performing house. Every item can also be performed by body: march the footsteps, groan the creak, tick-tock the tongue, drip the fingers.

Why this matters

The tap-faucet pair returns here in its splashiest form: a running tap is the house&rsquo;s loudest news. And the body-performance games make the words physical.

What it teaches

Sound-source reasoning (what made THAT?), onomatopoeia play (tip-tap, creak, tick-tock), and the detective habit of asking what the sound means.

Words to learn

footstepscreaky doorticking clockrunning tapringing phone

Say this to your child

“"Sounds around home! Tip-tap, creak, tick-tock, drip-drip, ring-ring — the house talks all day. What is it telling us right now?"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "the house plays music all day — here is the band."
  2. Perform each sound with your body: tip-tap feet, creeeak voice, tick-tock tongue, drip-drip fingers, ring-ring hands.
  3. Listen for real: which band member is playing right now? The clock is almost certainly on stage.
  4. The news game: what does a running tap say? (turn me off!) What do footsteps say? (someone is coming!)
  5. The tap check: is any tap dripping in the house? One walk, one listening tour, one hero.

Look closer at the picture

On this card the words "Sounds Around Home" sit over two blue footprints, an open door with motion lines by its hinge, a round ticking clock, a tap with a drop falling and a vintage phone mid-ring.

Ask your child

"What do footsteps tell us?" (someone is coming) "What does a running tap say?" (turn me off) "What says tick-tock all night?" (the clock)

What your child can say or do

Your child might announce every creak in the building, patrol the house for dripping taps like a plumber-in-chief, or perform the whole band on request.

Out in the real world

The listening habit lasts: a child who reads house sounds reads street sounds, classroom sounds, nature sounds. Ears trained at home stay trained.

Try it together

House Orchestra: the family performs the five sounds in a loop — footsteps, creak, tick-tock, drip, ring — faster and faster until it collapses into giggles. Then the quiet-minute hunt for the real versions.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does creeeak mean?" (a door is opening) "What is the tap saying when it runs?" (turn me off) "Who makes tip-tap?" (the footsteps — someone walking)

This lesson pairs with the Sounds Around Home flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Home and Daily Life.
